text: Last lesson covered Snowflake's general differences from T-SQL — LIMIT, double pipe, case folding, QUALIFY. This lesson zooms in on the single most distinctive piece of Snowflake syntax you'll meet in this entire course: the VARIANT type for semi-structured data. There is genuinely nothing in T-SQL that looks quite like this, so take your time with it.

VARIANT is a column type that can natively hold JSON, Avro, Parquet, or similar semi-structured data, without you declaring a fixed shape ahead of time. Create table events, event id int, payload VARIANT. Insert a row using PARSE underscore JSON to convert a JSON string literal into an actual VARIANT value. Nothing in T-SQL is structurally similar to this — T-SQL's closest answer, which we'll compare in a moment, treats JSON as plain text, not as its own native type.

To reach into a VARIANT column's fields, you start with a colon, then chain with dots or brackets. payload colon action gets you the top-level action field. payload colon user dot name reaches into a nested object. Bracket notation does the identical job — payload bracket quote user quote bracket quote name quote — and is especially useful when a key contains characters that would confuse the dot syntax. Notice it's a COLON that starts the path, not a dot; dots only come into play once you're chaining deeper.

Here's a subtlety worth knowing: whatever you pull out of a VARIANT path is ITSELF still a VARIANT value, not a plain string or number, until you explicitly cast it. That's what double-colon is for. payload colon user dot name double-colon STRING gives you an actual STRING. payload colon user dot age double-colon NUMBER gives you an actual NUMBER. Skip the cast, and comparisons or functions expecting a specific type may not behave the way you'd expect — the cast makes your intent explicit.

Now compare this to how T-SQL handles the same problem. T-SQL has no VARIANT-equivalent type — JSON lives as plain text inside an ordinary NVARCHAR column, and you read it with functions: JSON underscore VALUE of payload, dollar-sign dot user dot name. JSON_VALUE returns text, which you'd then cast yourself if you needed something else. Both approaches get you to the same data in the end — T-SQL leans on functions operating over a text column, while Snowflake gives semi-structured data a genuinely native, first-class type with its own dedicated path syntax.

To recap: VARIANT holds JSON, Avro, or Parquet natively; colon starts a path into it, dots and brackets chain deeper, and double-colon casts the result to a real scalar type. T-SQL's JSON functions operate on plain text instead of a native type — a genuinely structural difference, not just a naming one. Next lesson, we leave Snowflake behind and look at Databricks SQL and Spark SQL — a cloud warehouse platform with a very different heritage.
